summary: Daniel has a night vision in Belshazzar's first year: four strange animals rise from the sea, and the fourth is especially destructive, with a boastful horn. The scene shifts to a heavenly court where the Ancient of Days judges, and one like a son of man receives an everlasting dominion. Daniel is troubled, asks for an interpretation, and hears that the animals are kings or kingdoms, the saints will suffer under a hostile ruler, and then receive the kingdom.
whyItMatters: This chapter turns Daniel from court stories into symbolic visions while staying inside the Aramaic section of the book. It restates the book's central contrast: violent empires look overwhelming for a time, but their rule is limited before God's judgment.

context.author: The visions speak in Daniel's first-person voice. Traditional readings identify Daniel as author; many critical scholars see a second-century BC final composition using older Daniel traditions.
context.audience: Jews pressured to surrender worship, practice, identity, or hope under imperial power.
context.date: Narratively set in the sixth-century BC Babylonian world; many scholars date the final Hebrew-Aramaic form to about 167-164 BC during the crisis under Antiochus IV.
context.setting: The chapter is set in Babylon during the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon, while the book's visions reach toward later imperial persecution.
context.literaryForm: Apocalyptic vision with symbolic animals, heavenly judgment, numbered times, and an interpreting figure.

outline.heading: Daniel receives and records the vision
outline.note: The chapter begins with Daniel's dream in Belshazzar's first year, then shows four great animals rising from the sea.

outline.heading: The four animals and the arrogant horn
outline.note: Daniel sees a lionlike animal, a bearlike animal, a leopardlike animal, and a terrifying fourth animal with ten horns and another horn that speaks arrogantly.

outline.heading: The heavenly court and the humanlike figure
outline.note: The Ancient of Days sits in judgment, the fourth animal is destroyed, and one like a son of man receives dominion, glory, and an everlasting kingdom.

outline.heading: The first interpretation
outline.note: Daniel is troubled and asks for the truth; he is told the four animals are four kings, but the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom.

outline.heading: Daniel asks about the fourth animal
outline.note: Daniel focuses on the terrifying fourth animal, the ten horns, and the horn that wages war on the saints until judgment comes.

outline.heading: The fuller explanation and Daniel's reaction
outline.note: The fourth animal is explained as a fourth kingdom, the horns as kings, and the hostile ruler's dominion as temporary; Daniel remains deeply troubled and keeps the matter in his heart.

keyVerses.text: “I watched until thrones were placed, and one who was Ancient of Days sat. His clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool. His throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire.
keyVerses.why: This verse introduces the heavenly court, where the violent powers seen as animals are placed under judgment.

keyVerses.text: “I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they brought him near before him.
keyVerses.why: This is the chapter's central humanlike figure, contrasted with the beastlike kingdoms before him.

keyVerses.text: Dominion was given him, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion, which will not pass away, and his kingdom one that will not be destroyed.
keyVerses.why: The verse states the scope and permanence of the dominion given to the humanlike figure.

keyVerses.text: But the saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom, and possess the kingdom forever, even forever and ever.’
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the first explicit interpretation of the vision's outcome for the saints.

themes: arrogant speech against the Most High

questions.question: Where does this chapter fit in Daniel?
questions.answer: Daniel 7 begins the major vision section of the book, but it still belongs to the Aramaic block that runs through 7:28. The chapter is set in the first year of Belshazzar and presents Daniel himself receiving a dream rather than interpreting a king's dream.

questions.question: What are the four great animals?
questions.answer: The interpretation inside the chapter says, “These great animals, which are four, are four kings, who will arise out of the earth.” The text does not name all four in this chapter. Readers often connect them with sequences of empires in Daniel; those comparisons go beyond the identifications made here.

questions.question: Why does Daniel focus so much on the fourth animal?
questions.answer: The fourth animal is described as different, terrifying, and destructive, with iron teeth, bronze nails, and ten horns. Daniel asks especially about it because it is unlike the earlier animals and because another horn from it speaks arrogantly and attacks the saints.

questions.question: What does “horn” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: In the vision, horns are part of the fourth animal's appearance, but the interpretation identifies the ten horns as ten kings. Another horn arises after them, differs from the former kings, puts down three kings, and speaks against the Most High.

questions.question: Who is the Ancient of Days?
questions.answer: The chapter depicts the Ancient of Days as the enthroned figure in the heavenly court, surrounded by fire, attendants, judgment, and opened books. The text shows him judging arrogant and violent rule; it does not pause to define the title abstractly.

questions.question: Who is the one like a son of man?
questions.answer: The vision presents a humanlike figure who comes with the clouds of the sky, approaches the Ancient of Days, and receives dominion, glory, and a kingdom. The interpretation later says the saints receive and possess the kingdom, so readers differ over whether the figure is a corporate symbol for the holy people, an individual representative, or both together. Later Jewish and Christian readings develop this figure in different directions, but those later readings should not erase the chapter's own contrast between animals and a humanlike ruler.

questions.question: What happens to the saints in the chapter?
questions.answer: The saints are promised the kingdom, but not before conflict. The horn makes war with them and prevails for a time, then judgment is given to them and they possess the kingdom.

questions.question: What does “a time and times and half a time” mean?
questions.answer: The phrase marks a limited period during which the saints are given into the hostile ruler's hand. The chapter does not convert the phrase into a modern calendar date. Readers debate its precise calculation, but the immediate point is that the ruler's oppression has a boundary and is followed by judgment.

questions.question: Why is Daniel still troubled after receiving an interpretation?
questions.answer: The explanation clarifies the main symbols, but it also includes war against the saints, arrogant speech against the Most High, and a period of severe pressure. Daniel's reaction shows that receiving a vision and interpretation does not make the experience easy or emotionally settled.

glossary.def: A revealed scene Daniel sees at night; in this chapter it includes symbolic animals, heavenly judgment, and an interpretation.
The four great creatures in Daniel's dream; the chapter later says they represent four kings.
Parts of the fourth animal that are interpreted as kings, including another horn that speaks arrogantly and opposes the saints.
The enthroned figure in the heavenly court who appears when judgment is set.
The people of the Most High who suffer under the arrogant ruler and later receive the kingdom.
